candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Convert mixed numbers (and whole numbers when needed) into equivalent improper fractions with a specified denominator.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three experts define the same conversion operation: rewriting mixed numbers a b/c as (a·c+b)/c and optionally rewriting whole numbers as equivalent fractions with a chosen denominator.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Determine a common (often least common) denominator for fractions and rewrite each as an equivalent fraction over that denominator.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three experts describe selecting a common/LCM denominator and scaling numerators/denominators to produce equivalent fractions with matching denominators.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Compute the difference once quantities are in compatible form, typically by subtracting numerators over a common denominator and/or subtracting whole and fractional parts and combining the result.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A and B explicitly include subtracting mixed numbers by parts as well as common-denominator subtraction; C focuses on fraction subtraction over a common denominator (including already-equal denominators). These are the same core computation step (performing the subtraction), with A/B slightly broader phrasing.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Express the computed result in simplest accepted form by reducing fractions and/or converting between improper fractions, mixed numbers, and integers when appropriate.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three experts include reducing to lowest terms and normalizing the final form (e.g., converting improper to mixed, recognizing 0/3=0 or 8/8=1).

alignment_summary: Across the three codebooks, all skill_ids align cleanly into four shared concepts with full (3/3) consensus: converting mixed/whole numbers to improper fractions, finding a common denominator and generating equivalent fractions, performing the subtraction once forms are compatible, and simplifying/formatting the final result. No extra or unique (1/3) skills were present, and each expert’s S01–S04 mapped one-to-one to the same four concepts.
